slides.title: The HT16K33 and Its Device Driver
slides.subtitle: ENGS 28 · Day 10 — In-Class

slides.title: Where we are
items: Yesterday you used a bus: four wires, a program you were given, and four characters on your own display.
Today is everything that was handed to you — the chip at the far end of the two wires, the peripheral at our end, and the library call in between.

In that order: the display and its controller first, because that is where yesterday's unanswered questions are; then the STM32C031C6's own I2C1 peripheral; then the five operations a library has to provide.
By the end of the session your display shows ES.28, written out of a ten-byte buffer by a device driver you wrote. Lab 5 asks for that function.
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min with announcements. 110 minutes today, against 50 yesterday — say that, because the pace is genuinely different.

slides.title: Homework Review, and Two AI Solutions
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 9 min including the one-minute measurement that opens it (8 for the reading and the discussion). Individual written answer BEFORE the group talks, and a working reference copy offered to the whole room before groups form — so a student whose homework did not run has something to compare against and never has to say so out loud. First thing to compress to 6 min after Part 9; not to cut.

slides.title: Before you read anybody's code — measure your own
slides.body:
Your program from Tuesday prints once a second.

Time ten prints against a stopwatch and write down what you got.

Then write down the PSC and ARR your program uses.
slides.presenterNote: Costed inside Part 1's nine minutes, not on top of them. It is what makes the next ten minutes something an AI cannot do for them: two of the defects in the AI solutions are only visible if you know what clock this board runs at. Coolterm is already up; nobody needs to reflash. A student on the reference copy has a running program too.

What an I2C Library Has to Provide
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 6 min. Individually first, then the group, then the reveal. They have now called three of the five, so the derivation is grounded rather than abstract.

slides.title: Before we look at the library you were given
slides.body:
What operations does a program need in order to use this bus?

Aim for the smallest set that covers everything you have seen on the wire, and say for each one why it cannot be built out of the others.

One of them has nothing to do with any particular device. Which?
slides.presenterNote: Individually in writing, then compare at the table, then reveal. Do not accept 'read and write' — push for what the multi-byte forms need that the single-byte ones do not. They have already called init, byteWrite and memWrite, so two of the five should come straight out of their own program.

Recap
items: 34 LEDs on 14 wires, because a grid saves wires and a sweep buys back the one digit at a time it costs you. The backpack runs that sweep so your program does not have to — which is what you saw when you waved the display.
A device's commands come out of its datasheet's command table, one byte each, and the header's names are that table's structure.

Two bytes per digit position, five positions, and the odd bytes are what advance the HT16K33's pointer — which is why they have to be sent. All ten in ONE transaction, because a STOP ends the write and the next one starts over.
PB8 and PB9 are AF6, and open-drain is not a preference: SDA changes hands every ninth bit.
One assignment to I2C_CR2 describes an entire transaction. Nothing in the library counts a clock edge.
A device driver reaches the hardware only through the interface driver. A device driver may call i2c1_byteWrite() as often as it likes and may not touch I2C1->CR2 once.
The bus can be flawless and the device still do nothing. A scope answers 'did my bytes arrive?'; only the datasheet answers 'were they the right bytes?'
Tonight: the counters. The MM:SS clock is the one that makes you find the colon bit, and Lab 5 is the same shape.
